summary: A 1977 Telnet option for remote controlled transmission and echoing, so the server can control when the user's side sends characters and echoes them. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of sending every keypress, the far computer tells yours when to send and when to show letters. This note defines how.

questions: telnet remote controlled transmission and echoing
what is the telnet rcte option
how does remote controlled echoing work
what is a break character in telnet
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets the server tell your terminal when to send typed text and what to echo.

tldr.problem: Echoing every typed character back from a remote host wastes network traffic and, over a satellite link, adds long delays, while sending each keypress separately wastes more.
tldr.mechanism: With the RCTE option the server sends break reset commands that define which characters end a printing unit and which should prompt transmission, and the user Telnet buffers input and echoes locally by those rules.
tldr.outcome: Almost all server-to-user echoing goes away and fewer messages travel from user to server, but the option carries a rather large overhead and is meant only for full-duplex hosts.

today: RFC 726 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no RFC obsoleting or updating it. RFC 718 reports problems found when implementing it on TENEX.

sections.title: Why Control Echo Remotely
sections.content:
RFC 357, by John Davidson, introduced the problem of echo delay when a user reaches a full-duplex host over a satellite link. An echo control similar to that of some time-sharing systems is suggested for the entire network, so thousands of miles of transit are not paid for each echoed character.

The option has the using host regulate the local terminal printer by explicit instructions from the serving host. It also asks the using host to buffer terminal input until it forms a useful unit, so fewer messages go from user to server.

It is only intended for full-duplex hosts. The Go-Ahead feature is adequate for half-duplex servers. While RCTE is in use, Suppress Go-Ahead should be in force and the ECHO option should not be.
sections.eli5: Sending every letter across the ocean and waiting for it to bounce back is slow. This lets your own computer show the letters and send them in bigger bunches.

sections.title: Commands and the Control Byte
sections.content:
The option code is RCTE 7. WILL RCTE is sent by the controlling (serving) host, and DO RCTE by the host whose terminal printer is controlled. The control message is IAC SB RCTE <cmd> [BC1 BC2] [TC1 TC2] IAC SE, sent only by the controlling host, and is called a break reset command.

The <cmd> byte holds flags. Bit 0 set means act on the other bits; clear means repeat the last command. Bit 1 set skips echoing the break character. Bit 2 set skips echoing the text up to it. Bit 3 means two break class bytes follow, and bit 4 means two transmission class bytes follow. Even values above zero are in error and are treated as zero.

Classes are nine character groups, such as upper-case letters (class 1), format effectors (class 4) and space (class 9). A break character requires the user host to send all accumulated text and stop printing until the next break reset command. A transmission character only recommends sending. Initially no classes are in effect, and any Telnet command (IAC) acts as a break character except IAC IAC.
sections.eli5: The far computer sends a tiny note with switches on it: which letters mean 'send now' and whether to show the letters you typed.

sections.title: The Printing Procedure and Resynchronizing
sections.content:
Once the option is on, the user Telnet loops: read an item from the network, then handle terminal input. Data from the network is printed. A command sets the classes. Terminal items are printed or skipped as the latest command says, and when a break character is processed the cycle returns to waiting for the next command. Output the server sends at any time (spontaneous output) is printed while waiting for terminal input, and a command arriving then is an error.

For every break character the user sends, the server must send one break reset command, a one-to-one correspondence. To resynchronize, one side sends the Telnet Abort Output (AO) signal and the other answers with SYNCH and, from the server, a break reset command. The server should first be sure its output is printed, for example with the Timing Mark option.
sections.eli5: Each time you press a 'finish' key, the far computer must answer with new instructions. If the two get confused, they both stop, clear everything and start over.

sections.title: Buffering and Cautions
sections.content:
There are no mandatory transmission constraints. The using host may send a character at a time, though that wastes RCTE, and the transmission classes are only guidelines. The RFC notes RCTE entails a rather large overhead that is not justified for true character-at-a-time use, but on average should save network traffic and host wake-ups.

Typed-ahead text may contain break characters the user side cannot yet classify, so it may be sent but must wait to be printed until the next break reset command arrives. If the buffer fills and text will be lost, the user should be notified, perhaps by ringing the terminal bell. Defining no break characters other than Telnet commands is possible but undesirable. See RFC 718 for implementation experience.
sections.eli5: You might keep typing before the instructions arrive, so your computer has to hold on to what you typed. If its holding tray fills up, it should ring a bell.

items.label: Continue
items.desc: Continue what you have been doing.

items.label: Print all
items.desc: Print up to and including the break character.

items.label: Skip break
items.desc: Print up to the break character, but do not echo it.

items.label: Skip text
items.desc: Do not echo the text, but print the break character.

items.label: Skip both
items.desc: Skip up to and including the break character.

items.label: Break classes
items.desc: Add 8 to set break classes using the next two bytes.

items.label: Transmit classes
items.desc: Add 16 to set transmission classes using two more bytes.

items.label: Both
items.desc: Add 24 to set both break and transmission classes.
